newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Basque businessmen targeted in ETA strike.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Basque businessmen targeted in ETA strike.

text.p: Basque businessmen, who have long complained of intimidation by separatist group ETA, were divided in their response to a strike called by the rebels on Friday.
Large businesses defied the strike but many small shops stayed closed for fear of violent retaliation.

"Factories are working normally. The incidents of the strike are mainly in small businesses and commerce, mainly in the streets because they are afraid," said Jesus Mari Gabirondo, spokesman for the Guipuzcoa Entrepreneurs Association.
ETA's political arm Herri Batasuna (HB) declared the one-day general strike to protest at the imprisonment of its leadership but the regional government outlawed it on the grounds it was political.
Basque businesses said they had received threats warning them to heed the strike but business associations and unions denounced the call and urged people to ignore it.
Many small shops were closed while other nervous shopkeepers kept shutters half-open and stood outside to gauge the danger.
Pickets went door-to-door trying to enforce the strike and shattered some windows of open shops and banks. Increased police patrols alleviated some of the pressure.
Some shops decided to open on Saturday instead of Friday to avoid problems while a number stayed closed in solidarity with HB, which has a 10- to 15-percent popular following in the area.
Gabirondo said 95 percent of industries were operating normally and added he did not see any significant harm to the regional economy from the strike.
The Basque economy is industry-based with production concentrated in cars, machines, electronics and appliances.
"It's not a big loss economically. It's more the image of our industries and the Basque economy. We always give the image this is a country with problems in the streets," said Gabirondo.
There is particular concern foreign investors will shun the Basque country for other, less troubled regions of Spain.
For decades, Basque businessmen have said ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) demands payment of a "revolutionary tax" and frequently targets them for kidnappings and attacks.
ETA has killed some 800 people since 1968 in its campaign for an independent state. In the 1970s and 80s, some businessmen fled the region for safer ground.
"To be a businessman in the Basque country has its risks," said Enrique Portocarrero, director of the Circle of Basque Businessmen in Bilbao, the regional centre of commerce.
"The whole society is absolutely disgusted with this kind of violence," he added.

Businessmen say ETA, though small in numbers, is highly organised and effective in its extortion efforts. Through its labour union LAB, the group gathers financial information on companies used to calculate the "revolutionary tax" rate.
Four months ago, ETA took the son of a prominent and wealthy Basque business owner hostage. Officials and family of the prisoner, Cosme Delclaux, have said the motive was financial.
"Most people don't pay and hostages increase pressure on people to pay the revolutionary tax," Delclaux family spokesman Carmelo Renobales told Reuters. "They profit from the hostages."
